title: Mechanistic Insights into the Selective Electroreduction of Carbon Dioxide to Ethylene on Cu2O‐Derived Copper Catalysts
abstract: In this work, we made a comprehensive investigation to unravel the underlying causes for the selectivity of CO2 electroreduction toward ethylene on Cu2O-derived Cu catalysts. Scanning electron microscopy, Xray diffraction, cyclic voltammetry, chronoamperometry, chronopotentiometry, online gas chromatography, nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and numerical simulations of local pH were used toward this end. Ten Cu2O-derived Cu films of different thicknesses and morphologies were prepared and extensively characterized. Aqueous 0.1 M KHCO3 was used as the electrolyte. We report here, for the first time, a remarkably strong correlation between the statistically relevant crystallite sizes of the Cu2O-derived Cu particles and selective CO2 electroreduction to C2H4. Specifically, as the crystallite size of the particles decreased from 41 to 18 nm, the Faradaic efficiency (FE) of C2H4 formation increased from 10 to 43%. Using cyclic voltammetry, samples with smaller particle crystallite sizes were found to possess more diverse adsorption sites for CO (a known reaction intermediate), which we interpret to be important for the C−C coupling of C1 adsorbates to C2 intermediates. The effect of local pH on the yield of C2H4 for the different Cu2O-derived Cu catalysts was less significant when compared to the effects of crystallite sizes and mass transport limitations. We also show here that remarkable amounts of C2 and C3 products could be achieved using these Cu2O-derived Cu catalysts. Driven at a fixed total current density of −31.2 mA cm−2, the catalysts could reduce CO2 to C2H4, ethanol, and npropanol with optimized FEs of 42.6% (jC2H4 = −13.3 mA cm−2), 11.8% (jC2H5OH = −3.7 mA cm−2), and 5.4% (jC3H7OH = −1.7 mA cm−2), respectively.

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
The electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide using green electricity presents a viable opportunity to mitigate the greenhouse effect caused by spiraling anthropogenic CO2 emissions, while providing a sustainable supply of chemical feedstocks and fuels for our needs.1 To date, copper is the only metal that could electroreduce CO2 to substantial amounts of high value and energy-dense products, such as methane, ethylene, ethanol and n-propanol.2−7 However, the selectivity, stability, and energetic efficiency of this electrocatalytic process need to be optimized before it can be deployed widely in the industries. Among the CO2 reduction catalysts that have been developed, copper oxide-derived Cu films have attracted attention due to their remarkable selectivity toward C2 and C3 products.
5−9 These catalysts are typically produced by heating copper films/substrates,10 or by electrodepositing copper oxide particles directly onto working electrodes.5
They can then be placed into the electrolytic cell, where they are rapidly reduced to Cu0 films during CO2 reduction at cathodic potentials. This process typically gives Cu catalysts with considerable porosity, high surface areas and roughness
all of which have been shown to affect overall current density and local pH.5,9,11,12 Thus, it is not surprising that these films reduce CO2 differently as compared to bulk metallic copper electrodes. Frese Jr. performed pioneering work of CO2 reduction on Cu2O films, and claimed the catalytic formation of methanol. 13 Subsequently, Le et al. reported similarly that electrodeposited Cu2O films could catalyze CO2 reduction to methanol in aqueous 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte with a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 38%.12 Cu1+ sites present in these films were proposed to be catalytically involved. On the other hand, Li et al. found that on >3 μm thick Cu2O-derived Cu 0 films, CO2 reduced to CO (FE ∼ 45%), and formic acid (FE 30%) at overpotentials between 0.19−0.39 V and 0.25−0.45 V, respectively. At higher overpotentials of 0.8−0.9 V, ethanol and ethylene were formed with maximum FEs of 4.7 and 3.9%, respectively.10 No methanol was detected. More recently, Kas et al. as well as our group showed that Cu2O-derived Cu films could reduce

CO2 to ethylene under ambient pressure conditions with even higher FEs of 34−39%.5,9 Less than 1% methane was formed, and thus a high FEC2H4/FECH4 ratio (i.e., selectivity) of ∼100 could be achieved. Notably, we also discovered that significant amounts of ethanol could be simultaneously produced with FEs of 9−16%. The causes for the enhanced formation of C2H4 on these films have been attributed to a myriad of factors, such as an increase in local pH at the surface of the electrode during reaction, thickness of the films, and the presence of (100)Cu facets and defect sites.5,9,14,15 High-resolution transmission electron microscopy on a limited number of catalyst nanoparticles have identified some of these defect sites as grain boundaries.16 The presence of these sites may have enhanced the adsorption of C1 reaction intermediates on the catalyst, which will in turn facilitate their intermolecular C−C bond formation to give C2 and C3 products.
4 Recently, thermal desorption studies under ultrahigh vacuum conditions supported this postulate by identifying strongly chemisorbed CO on Cu2O-derived Cu.
16 Residual CuOx species have also been proposed to be involved in the catalytic reduction of CO2 to C2H4.
17 However, evidence from simultaneous linear sweep voltammetry and online mass spectrometry during CO2 reduction has indicated that no products were formed from Cu2O surfaces.
9 Our in situ Raman spectroscopy data also showed that these oxide surfaces, upon application of the cathodic potentials necessary for CO2 electroreduction, reduced to metallic Cu0 within several minutes.5
In this work, we extensively investigate the underlying factors determining the selectivity of CO2 reduction to ethylene on Cu2O-derived Cu films. Aqueous 0.1 M KHCO3 was used as the electrolyte. Catalysts films of various thicknesses and morphologies were first prepared by hydrothermal synthesis. The effects of local pH and morphology on the selectivity of C2H4 formation were then investigated. We propose to use the crystallite sizes of the catalysts (determined from XRD) as a statistically relevant descriptor to explain their selectivity. Specifically, we show here that the selectivity of CO2 reduction, particularly toward C2H4, is strongly correlated to the crystallite sizes of the Cu2O-derived Cu particles. Cyclic voltammetry studies using CO as a probe molecule revealed that catalyst particles with smaller crystallite sizes tend to have a higher availability and more diverse coordination sites for CO adsorption. Their catalytic role in the selective formation of C2H4 is proposed and discussed in this work.

sections.heading: 2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
sections.text:
Synthesis. Ten Cu2O samples, named A to J, were prepared (see Table 1).18 The Cu2O films were grown hydrothermally onto mechanically polished Cu discs (99.99%, 10 mm diameter, Goodfellow) suspended on a custom-made Teflon holder in a Teflon-lined stainless steel autoclave (Parr 4744, Parr Instruments) at 145 °C for 90 min. A precursor solution consisting of 0.25 M of Cu(NO3)2·3H2O (99.7%, Sigma-Aldrich) and 0− 1.75 M NH3 dissolved in a solvent was used. The solvent consisted of a 23:13:2 volumetric ratio of ethanol (absolute, Merck): ultrapure water (≥18.2 mΩ·cm, Barnstead): formic acid (98%, Sigma-Aldrich). The thickness of the films was expected to increase with the concentration of the NH3.
18 The as-prepared Cu2O films were then washed with copious amounts of water, dried overnight at 60 °C and prereduced to Cu0 in a separate 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte for 300 s, before being used as catalysts for CO2 reduction. We termed these as Cu2O-derived Cu. Loose Cu2O powder formed during the synthesis of the Cu2O film was also collected and spread onto chemically resistant 15 mm diameter Ti discs. These were then reduced at the same conditions as the above-mentioned films, and analyzed with X-ray diffraction to give parameters such as crystallite sizes and microstrains.
Materials Characterization by X-ray Diffraction and Scanning Electron Microscopy. Diffraction patterns of the films were collected using a Siemens 5005 diffractometer (40 kV, 40 mA, Cu Kα radiation with graphite monochromator). To minimize signals from the Cu disc substrate, detector-scan mode with a fixed incoming X-ray angle of 4° off the surface was used to scan the films from 15 to 100° 2θ with 0.02° stepsize, 1° fixed divergence slit, and at 1 s per step. Cu crystallite size and microstrain were calculated from the integral breadth of every Cu0 XRD peak of the reduced Cu2O powder (spread on Ti substrate). Gonio scan mode was used to scan these powder samples from 20 to 145° 2θ range with 0.02° step-size, 6.6 mm variable divergence slit, and 1 s per step. The use of variable divergence slit and long-range was necessary to maximize the signal intensity at higher 2θ and decouple the effects of size and strain broadening, respectively.19 X-ray data treatment and calculation were performed on Bruker Topas 4.2 using both Rietveld and whole powder pattern decomposition method in fundamental parameter mode.20 More details on the refinement strategy are presented in Section S1 of the Supporting Information (SI). The morphology, shape and size of the catalysts were further characterized by field emission
DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpcc.6b07128 J. Phys. Chem. C XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
B
scanning electron microscopy (JEOL JSM-6710 F, 5 keV, 10 μA). Electrochemistry. Electrochemical measurements were
performed using a Gamry 600 galvanostat/potentiostat using a three-electrode configuration. The electrodes were housed in a custom-made, gastight, two compartment Teflon cell.21 A Ag/ AgCl (Saturated KCl, Pine Research Instrumentation) and a Pt wire (ALS Japan) were used respectively as the reference and counter electrode. The potential of the Ag/AgCl reference electrode was checked daily against a reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE, HydroFlex, Gaskatel). All potentials reported in this work were referenced against the RHE. The anodic and cathodic compartments were separated by an anion-exchange membrane (Selemion AMV, AGC Asahi Glass). A holder gripped the working electrode firmly in place and exposed only a circular geometric surface area of 0.385 cm2. Unless otherwise stated, all reported current densities were normalized to the exposed geometric surface area of the working electrode. The cathodic compartment was filled with 10 mL electrolyte, leaving 2 mL of headspace. Before each measurement, the aqueous 0.1 M KHCO3 (99.97%, Merck Millipore) electrolyte was saturated with CO2 gas (99.999%, Linde Gas) for 30 min. All experiments were performed at 298 K. CO2 was pumped into the catholyte and anolyte during the CO2 reduction process at a rate of 20 sccm using mass flow controllers (MC-100SCCM-D, Alicat Scientific). The gas outlet of the cathodic compartment was connected to a gas chromatograph (GC-7890A, Agilent) for periodical sampling. The GC is equipped with a thermal conductivity detector for detecting H2 and flame ionization detectors with a methaniser for detecting hydrocarbons and CO. The carrier gases for the TCD and FIDs are nitrogen and helium, respectively. A typical CO2 electroreduction experiment at a constant applied potential or current spanned over 4240 s. Gas aliquots were injected into the GC every 11 min by an automated sampler. The first injection was made 200 s after the start of the CO2 reduction reaction. Seven gas samples were analyzed. However, to ensure that the reported data is from a system under equilibrium conditions, only the average of the fifth, sixth, and seventh GC measurements was used in the data analysis. After each CO2 electroreduction experiment, 2 mL of the catholyte was mixed with 0.1 mL of an internal standard consisting of 25 mM phenol (99.6%, VWR) and 5 mM dimethyl sulfoxide (99.9%, Quality Reagent Chemical). 0.1 mL D2O (99.96% deuterium, Merck Millipore) was then added to 0.5 mL of this mixture. The liquid CO2 reduction products therein were analyzed by 1H NMR, with the use of a solvent suppression protocol to decrease the intensity of the water peak (average of 64 scans, Avance DRX 500 MHz, Bruker). The results were processed using Bruker TopSpin and MestReNova (V9.0.1, Mestrelab Research S.L.) software. The electrochemical active surface areas (ECSAs) of the
Cu2O-derived Cu catalysts were estimated by double layer capacitance measurements from 0.01 to 0.1 V s−1 in N2-purged 0.1 M NaF electrolyte (pH 6.8). A specific capacitance of 28 μF cm−2 was assumed for a smooth Cu surface.22
The film thickness was estimated from the total charge delivered during the prereduction process of the Cu2O films in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte (SI Section S2). A one-electron reduction for Cu1+ + e− → Cu0 was assumed. The density of the Cu0 film was taken as 8.96 g cm−3.23
Numerical Simulations. Numerical calculations were performed (using MATLAB 8.5) to estimate the concentration profiles of CO2, HCO3 −, CO3 2−, OH−, as well as the local pH within the diffusion layer. The method and equations employed by Gupta et al. were used.24 The electrochemical active surface areas of the catalysts were taken into account during the calculations.

sections.heading: 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
3.1. Characterization of As-Grown Cu2O and Cu2ODerived Cu Films. After synthesis, the morphologies, particle sizes, chemical compositions, thickness, electrochemical active surface areas, microstrains (εo) and crystallite sizes of Samples A to J were determined (Figure 1 and Table 1). SEM images of four representative Cu2O samples (Samples A, C, E, and J, before CO2 reduction) are presented in Figures 1(a, c, e, g). The average sizes of the particles increase with the amount of NH3 added to the precursor solution, and are 0.5−1, 3−6, 5−8 and 10−20 μm for Samples A, C, E, and J, respectively. In this work, the effect of increasing NH3 concentration during synthesis caused the Cu2O to appear as a rectification sequence, transiting from (100)Cu2O (cuboid, Sample A, Figure 1a) to (110)Cu2O (manifested as rhombuses along the [100] spines of the cuboids, Sample C, Figure 1c) and finally (111)Cu2O (octahedron, Samples E and J, Figures 1e and 1g). This is consistent with previous observations made on the growth of Cu2O powder using the same method. 18,25
These Cu2O particles were then prereduced, and used as catalysts for CO2 reduction at −0.98 V. At the end, the micronsized Cu2O particles were found to convert to aggregates of 40−200 nm sized Cu2O-derived Cu nanoparticles (Figures 1b,d,f,h). We could not discern from these SEM images any systematic change in sizes of the particles. The observation of aggregated Cu particles after reduction is consistent with the dissolution-diffusion-nucleation-coalescence process that occurs during the electrochemical reduction of copper oxides.26 The irregular shapes of the Cu2O-derived Cu particles suggest that Cu formation occurred under diffusion control,27 which is expected as the reduction potential is sufficiently negative and the Cu source is limited to the initial Cu2O film. Cracks visible through the catalyst films may be attributed to the relief of structural strains during the reduction of Cu2O.
28,29 Samples A to J were estimated to be between 1.3 and 11.2 μm thick, with the thinnest and thickest being Samples A and J, respectively (Table 1, SI Section S2). X-ray diffraction of the films demonstrate that the assynthesized Cu2O particles reduced to metallic Cu 0 after the reduction process, which agrees with predictions from the Pourbaix diagram of copper (Figure 1i).30 We also derive the crystallite sizes of the Cu2O-derived Cu particles from their respective diffractograms. These vary from 18 to 41 nm (Table 1). Interestingly, these sizes are not directly proportional to the thickness or roughness of the films. Rather, they can be related to the facet composition of the as-grown Cu2O film. Smaller Cu crystallites were observed on catalysts with more (110)Cu2O facets (Sample C), while larger ones were observed on (111)Cu2O dominated facets (Samples E and J). This can be attributed to the Cu atoms nucleating with a similar orientation as the underlying Cu2O facet (due to the better lattice match).31,32 The difference in crystallite sizes can then be explained by the growth preference. Face-centered cubic metals like Cu tend to grow along the energetically more favorable facets of {111} and {100} (as compared to {110}), which thus
DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpcc.6b07128 J. Phys. Chem. C XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
C
yields larger crystals on these orientations.33 The microstrains for Samples A to J were calculated to be 0.13−0.25% (Table 1). Here, it should be noted that the crystallite sizes and microstrains of each type of Cu2O-derived Cu samples (A, B, C, ..., or J) were not found to differ significantly, even when different reduction potentials were applied. 3.2. Selective Reduction of CO2 on Cu2O-Derived Cu Catalysts. Electrochemistry and Quantification of Products. The electrochemical reduction of CO2 using Samples A−J was performed in 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte, and their representative chronoamperograms (measured at −0.98 V) are presented in Figure 2a. The current densities exhibited by the Cu catalysts generally increased with the thickness of the films (from Samples A to J), which also scaled with their electrochemical
active surface areas (Table 1). The application of more cathodic potentials on the electrodes expectedly drove larger currents (Figure 2b). Fluctuations in the currents could be ascribed to the dynamic build-up and release of gas bubbles at the surface of the electrode during the CO2 reduction, which blocks/frees catalytic sites. The Faradaic efficiencies of the carbonaceous products formed during CO2 reduction on Samples A−J at various electrochemical potentials are presented in Figure 3 (and SI Section S3). H2 gas was also produced from the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER, 2H+ + 2e− → H2). The key observations made with these Cu2O-derived Cu catalysts were the significant production of C2H4 (max FE 31%) and ethanol (max FE 16%), and suppression of CH4 formation to 1−2%. C2H4 was generally produced together with ethanol, albeit with higher Faradaic efficiencies. It is also notable that while the FE of C2H4 maximized at lower overpotentials for thicker films, they were not higher. For example, the maximum FEC2H4 for the thickest sample, i.e., Sample J, was significantly lower at 15% (E = −0.83 V), compared to the maximum FEC2H4 for Sample C at 31% (E = −0.98 V). These observations are generally consistent with those made earlier by Li, Kas et al. and our group on Cu2O-derived Cu catalysts.
5,9,10 Unlike the studies by Frese Jr. and Le et al. on oxidized Cu,12,13 we could not detect any catalytic production of methanol. This could be because our reduced Cu films, as indicated by XRD, did not contain any detectable amount of Cu2O (we could not though, exclude the possibility that trace amounts of amorphous oxides may have evaded detection by XRD). Zhang and Peterson had also previously shown, on the basis of density functional theory calculations, that the reduction of CH3O* intermediates to CH3OH is thermodynamically more favored on oxidized rather than metallic Cu sites.34
Control experiments using N2 feed gas instead of CO2 were also performed (SI Section S3). Only H2 was found. This demonstrates that the carbonaceous products detected in this work originate from the electreoreduction of CO2, rather than from contamination.
Effect of Local pH. The selective reduction of CO2 to C2H4 on Cu2O-derived Cu catalysts has been attributed to a combination of two factors: (i) an increase in local pH at the surface of the electrode and (ii) morphological (structuralsensitive) factors.3,5,9,11,35 As shown by Gupta et al., local pH typically increased as total current density (jtot) increased (due to the consumption of CO2 and H
+ to give H2 and/or carbonaceous products).24 Thus, to study the effect of local pH on the selectivity of C2H4 formation, we plot the FEC2H4 versus average jtot of the samples (using data from the chronoamperometry experiments in SI Section S3). It is revealing that FEC2H4 versus jtot profiles of each sample followed a Gaussianlike function and shared a common FEC2H4 peak position around −25 to −35 mA cm−2 (Figure 4). The increase of FEC2H4 as jtot increased (left arm of the curve) may be explained by concurrent rise in applied overpotentials (a high η drives a larger cathodic current) and local pH at the surface of the electrode. The FE of C2H4 declined as jtot exceeded −25 to −35 mA cm−2 (even though local pH is expected to rise further; right arm of the curve). This decline is coupled with the concomitant increase of jCH4 and jH2 rate, indicating that both H2 and CH4 productions are becoming more favorable over C2H4 formation as jtot increased (SI Section S4). The phenomenon can be understood as follows: at these very cathodic potentials, the
DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpcc.6b07128 J. Phys. Chem. C XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
D
surface coverage of adsorbed CO (or other C1 moieties) will decrease as a result of their rapid reaction (to carbonaceous molecules) and departure from the catalyst. Thus, it becomes statistically more likely for a C1 intermediate to undergo proton/electron transfers to CH4, rather than undergo intermolecular C−C coupling to give a C2 dimer. The lower CO coverage will in turn free up hitherto inaccessible Cu sites for the H2 evolution reaction (which explains why H2 formation was observed to increase as ethylene formation decreased).5,21
Jaramillo and co-workers have also previously reported that HER and CH4 formation become more prevalent at negative potentials on polycrystalline Cu surfaces.2 Mass transport limitations of CO2 to these electrodes at high jtot (jCO2RR) will
also result in lower CO2 reduction and C2H4 production (SI Section S4).36
It is notable that the maximum FEC2H4 that could be achieved for Samples C (32%) > E (27%) ≈ A (25%) > J (13%) (Figure 4). If the local pH is the dominant factor in influencing their selectivity toward C2H4 formation, similar selectivity should have been expected, especially for Samples A, C, and E.9 This is because these three surfaces have similar ECSAs of 33.6, 37.1, and 34.3 cm2, respectively (Table 1), and hence should exhibit similar local pH values at the same jtot. 24
These findings and analyses indicate that local pH may not be solely used to explain the variation of C2H4 yields on different Cu samples. The determining factor for the selectivity
DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpcc.6b07128 J. Phys. Chem. C XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
E
of the CO2 reduction could also be related to the structure and size of the catalyst, as has been shown on single crystal and nanoparticulate Cu surfaces.14,37
Crystallite Size of Particles as Activity Descriptor. Here, we propose, for the first time, to correlate the selectivity of CO2 reduction to the crystallite sizes of the Cu2O-derived Cu particles. A crystallite is defined as a region with a regular crystalline arrangement, which could either be a single crystalline nanoparticle or a grain in a polycrystalline material. Unlike electron microscopy techniques, obtaining the crystallite size of a sample through X-ray diffraction is much more straightforward and statistically significant, as the value derived from a single measurement is an average of a large number of crystallites within the scanned sample area (∼61 mm2).38 Chronopotentiometry on the Cu2O-derived Cu particles at a constant current density of −31.2 mA cm−2 was performed. This value was selected as it is around the midpoint of the common FEC2H4 peak observed during chronoamperometric measurements (Figure 4). We note that FEC2H4 of Sample E has just started to decline at this current density, but the effect of mass transport is expected to be very limited. The measured FEC2H4 and jC2H4 of the 10 samples were then plotted as a function of their crystallite sizes (Figure 5). The most striking observation here is that the FEC2H4 (or jC2H4) and crystallite sizes of the Cu2O-derived Cu samples can be linearly correlated. Specifically, as the crystallite size of the particles decreases from 41 to 18 nm, the FE of C2H4 increases from 10 to 43%. Of great practical significance is also the high partial current density of C2H4 at −13.3 mA cm−2. Previous works have suggested the use of physical characteristics such as film thickness9,11 and microstrain39 as activity descriptors for the activity of CO2 or CO reduction. However, we have not obtained any compelling reasons to believe that these factors are dominating in this work. This is evidenced by the low correlation factor and the poor linearity with respect to FEC2H4 (SI Section S5). We further note that the Cu2O-derived Cu films prepared in this work were formed through the in situ reduction of Cu2O. This occurred through a dissolutionnucleation process,26 which allowed relief of microstrains through plastic deformations.40 This is evident by the cracks visible through the catalyst films.29 Thus, it is not surprising that no strong correlation could be drawn between the
microstrains of Samples A−J and their selectivity toward ethylene formation (SI Section S5).
Numerical Simulations of Local pH at Electrode Surfaces. We also use numerical simulations to examine the relationship between the local pH at the catalyst surfaces during CO2 reduction with their selectivity toward ethylene (SI Section S6).24 The partial current densities of all products, concentrations of OH−, CO2, CO3 2−, and HCO3 −, and the ECSAs were taken into account. We simplify the calculations by using a planar electrode surface as model with a continuous diffusion layer. The FEC2H4 and jC2H4 measured at −31.2 mA cm−2 (geometric) were then plotted against the simulated local pH and ECSAs (SI Section S6). These variables were not found to be strongly correlated. This confirms that the different selectivities of the Cu2O-derived Cu films toward ethylene could be more strongly attributed to morphological factors rather than local pH.
3.3. Probing the Active Sites of Cu Catalysts by Cyclic Voltammetry. This brings us to the most pertinent question: why are Cu2O-derived Cu films with smaller crystallite sizes more effective for producing C2H4? We turn to cyclic voltammetry to characterize the CO2 reduction active sites in the samples. CO was chosen as a probe molecule since it is a well-known intermediate of CO2 reduction to ethylene.
35 0.1 M NaF electrolyte was used as the ions are weakly adsorbed on Cu, and thus less likely to compete with CO for adsorption sites.41 In CO-saturated NaF electrolyte, the onset of the cathodic current was generally shifted to more negative potentials (relative to the experiments done in N2-purged electrolyte). This can be attributed to the stronger adsorption of CO (vs H) on the Cu surfaces, which is expected to delay the evolution of H2 gas (SI section S7).
42 It is also notable that the onset potential for the thickest Sample J was earlier by ∼100 mV. This observation is consistent with the earlier formation of C2H4 during CO2 reduction (Figure 3 and SI Section S3). In excellent agreement with previous CO adsorption studies on poly- and single- crystal Cu surfaces, we observed CO adsorption (cathodic) peaks on our Cu2O-derived Cu samples at around −0.3 to −0.5 V (Figure 6).41,43,44 Even more
DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpcc.6b07128 J. Phys. Chem. C XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
F
interestingly, different adsorption profiles were observed. Smaller crystallite-sized samples had more complex CO adsorption profiles (Figure 6a), with at least three distinct adsorption peaks at −0.51, −0.40, and −0.29 V being identified for Sample C (the smallest crystallite size). As the crystallite size increases, these adsorption sites merge to form a simpler two-peaks profile at around −0.46 and −0.23 V (for Sample J, which has the largest crystallite size). It is challenging to assign the observed CV peaks because
these do not coincide with those of (100)Cu, (111)Cu, and (110)Cu (SI Section S7). Considering the highly corrugated and irregularly shaped Cu2O-derived Cu particles examined in this study (Figure 1), it is reasonable to assign such peak features to the adsorption of CO on highly defective Cu sites. The more complex features are interpreted as a sign of the higher diversity and availability of CO adsorption sites on samples with smaller crystallites. An integration of the charges beneath these cathodic peaks would thus be an indicator of the surface population of CO. While we are aware that it is unlikely for CV to detect all the CO species present, reliable estimates of the CO population on all the catalysts can be obtained with the
consistent use of this method (assuming equal number of electron transfer for each adsorbed CO).45 A linear correlation was observed when we plot FEC2H4 observed at −31.2 mA cm−2 versus the charge under the cathodic peaks of CO adsorption for Samples A to J (Figure 6b). This clearly suggests that the population of adsorption sites for CO is directly linked to the activity and selectivity of CO2 reduction to C2H4. These results are also in excellent agreement with a previous study of CO adsorption on CuCl-derived Cu mesocrystals, Cu nanoparticles and polycrystalline Cu surfaces.21 Copper mesocrystals, which exhibited optimized selectivity toward CO2 reduction to C2H4, were found to adsorb CO more readily than the other two Cu catalysts. Based on previous experimental and theoretical works, the
mechanism for CO2 reduction to ethylene can be described as follows: CO2 is first reduced to adsorbed C1 intermediates such as CO(ad) or protonated CHxO(ad) (for example, CHO(ad)).
15,35,46,47 If these intermediates are sufficiently stabilized on the catalyst’s surface, their concentration would build up. This would directly facilitate their C−C coupling to give C2 adsorbates, which are then further hydrogenated to
DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpcc.6b07128 J. Phys. Chem. C XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
G
produce C2H4. We propose here that the adsorption and stabilization of these intermediates are significantly enhanced on Cu2O-derived Cu, especially on particles with smaller crystallite sizes. Aggregates of these smaller particles are likely to give rise to a higher surface population of catalytically active sites situated on grain boundaries, defects and particle−particle junctions. This proposition is supported by the work of Verdaguer-Cassadevall et al., which demonstrated the presence of strongly chemisorbed CO on sites supported by grain boundaries.16 The present findings also agree with our previous study of CO2 reduction on Cu nanocrystals, whose excellent activity toward ethylene, ethanol, and n-propanol formation can be attributed to their small particle sizes of ∼15 nm.7 However, we reiterate here that the findings from X-ray diffraction data are statistically more relevant than electron microscopy studies that focused only on a handful of crystals. While the crystallite size was found to be linearly correlated to FEC2H4 (or jC2H4) throughout this study, a different trend may be observed on particles with very small crystallite sizes. We note here that Reske et al. have previously shown that small 2 nm-sized Cu nanoparticles are less selective for CO2 reduction to hydrocarbons.37 This has been ascribed to the decreased surface mobility of the adsorbed CO and H intermediates, which reduced their recombination. 3.4. Optimization of C2 and C3 Product Yield Using Chronopotentiometry. The yield of CO2 reduction products for a particular catalyst is commonly optimized by tuning the applied overpotential until a high FE is achieved.10,48 However, a high FE does not always equate to high partial current density.7 The latter is arguably a more practical figure of merit in determining the usefulness of a catalyst. In this section, we demonstrate that fine-tuning of C2 and C3 products distribution for our catalysts can be achieved through chronopotentiometry at various fixed currents. For this purpose, Sample C, which is the best performing catalyst for CO2 reduction to C2H4, was chosen as an illustration (Figure 7). Reducing or increasing the applied current density from the reference point of −31.2 mA cm−2 to −28.6 or −39 mA cm−2 resulted in a decrease of overall CO2 reduction products, in particular C2H4, C2H5OH, and npropanol (C3H7OH). These three compounds are known to form through similar reaction pathways.2,35 At ambient pressure, the FEs (and partial current densities) could be optimized to 70.1% (−21.9 mA cm−2) for total CO2 reduction products, 42.6% (−13.3 mA cm−2) for C2H4, 11.8% (−3.7 mA cm−2) for C2H5OH and 5.4% (−1.7 mA cm−2) for C3H7OH, respectively. These figures-of-merit are comparable, if not much better than many previously reported values for CO2 reduction to C2H4 (−0.6 to −11.9 mA cm−2),2,5,9,10,17,21 C2H5OH (−0.7 to −5.7 mA cm−2)2,5,10 and C3H7OH (−0.2 to −1.74 mA cm−2)2,7,10 on Cu-based catalysts at room temperature and pressure. We note that a CO2 reduction study on oxide-derived Cu nanoparticles by Kas et al. had reported a similar FE of 43% for C2H4, albeit under the condition of CO2 pressure of 9 atm.11
Our present findings strongly demonstrate that reducible metal composites such as Cu2O-derived Cu is a leading choice as electrocatalyst for efficient CO2 reduction. Small Cu crystallites, obtained from the in situ reduction of Cu2O, were found to exhibit superior activity and selectivity toward higher carbon chain products such as ethylene. We further note that earlier works on oxide-derived films have tried to relate the variability in C2 products formation to factors such as
thickness5,9 or grain boundary/defect termination.6,16 We have undertaken a more comprehensive investigation into these various physical and electrochemical aspects of CO2 electroreduction, and pinpointed that the improved C2 products selectivity on Cu2O-derived Cu is best correlated with its crystallite size. In the light of the present work, we have proposed that these films could be examined by X-ray diffraction, and the crystallite sizes of the particles is a statistically relevant and practical parameter to describe their selectivity and activity. The present findings are critical steps toward the use of Cu2O-derived Cu as industrial catalysts for producing useful chemical feedstocks and fuels from CO2 building blocks.

sections.heading: 4. CONCLUSION
sections.text:
In this work, we extensively investigate the factors determining the selectivity of CO2 reduction to ethylene on Cu2O-derived Cu films. We show that the crystallite size of the Cu particles is an ideal descriptor as it forms a predictable relationship with CO2 reduction activity toward ethylene and is easy to determine accurately. It is also demonstrated that particles with smaller crystallite size have higher availability and more diverse sites for CO adsorption. We also show that CO2 mass transport and CH4 formation/H2 evolution become more prevalent at current densities above −25 to −35 mA cm−2. Finally, optimum amounts of C2 and C3 products could be achieved using these catalysts. At a fixed total current density of −31.2 mA cm−2, the C2H4, C2H5OH, C3H7OH, and total CO2 reduction FE could be optimized to 42.6% (jC2H4 = −13.3 mA cm−2), 11.8% (jC2H5OH = −3.7 mA cm−2), 5.4% (jC3H7OH = −1.7 mA cm−2), and 70.1% (jCO2RR = −21.9 mA cm−2), respectively.
